title_en: Botan Company v. Xiamen Customs — dispute over administrative penalty decision
ruling_gist_en: 1. A warehousing enterprise as a legal person that has a duty to examine the source of goods under customs supervision, who knows that others are smuggling goods, and although has repeatedly indicated to the smuggler its refusal to provide warehousing services for smuggled goods, has in fact continuously provided warehousing services for such goods without reporting to the customs, thereby violating Article 6, paragraph 2 of the Regulations of the People's Republic of China on the Implementation of Customs Administrative Penalties and constituting joint smuggling.
keywords_en: Administrative; Administrative Penalty; First Instance; Intermediate People's Court; Fujian Province; Legal Person; Regulations of the People's Republic of China on the Implementation of Customs Administrative Penalties; Determination of Joint Smuggling; Applicability of Former Implementing Rules; Composition of Illegal Gains; Dismissal of Claims; Smuggling; Warehousing Services; Knowing Non-Reporting; Administrative Litigation; Dispute over Administrative Penalty Decision by Xiamen Customs
full_text_en:
Botan Co., Ltd. v. Xiamen Customs — Dispute over Administrative Penalty Decision

[Ruling Summary]

1. A warehousing enterprise法人 that has a duty to examine the source of goods under Customs supervision, which knowingly stores smuggled goods for others, and although it repeatedly expresses refusal to provide warehousing services for the smuggled goods to the smugglers, in fact continuously provides such services without reporting to the Customs, its conduct violates Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Implementing Rules for Administrative Penalties under the Customs Law of the People's Republic of China, and constitutes joint smuggling.

2. Where an administrative agency, for the purpose of implementing a law, formulates implementing rules, regulations, or other administrative regulations based on that law, after the relevant law is amended, such administrative regulations remain applicable so long as they have not been expressly repealed by a law, an administrative regulation, or the enacting authority, and are not inconsistent with the amended law.

3. An administrative penalty of confiscation of illegal gains and imposition of a fine against a person who, with knowledge of the facts, fails to report and provides convenience to smugglers is consistent with Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Implementing Rules for Administrative Penalties under the Customs Law of the People's Republic of China. The argument of the penalized party, citing provisions of other documents, that the costs it incurred should be deducted from the illegal gains, is untenable.

Plaintiff: Fujian Xiamen Botan Warehousing Co., Ltd., domiciled at: Haicang Songyu, Xiamen City.
Legal Representative: Chen Hehua, Chairman of the Board.

Defendant: Xiamen Customs, People's Republic of China, domiciled at: Haihou Road, Xiamen City.
Legal Representative: Zhou Zhuowei, Director of the Customs.

The plaintiff, Xiamen Botan Warehousing Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Botan Company), dissatisfied with the administrative penalty decision made against it by the defendant, Xiamen Customs of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as Xiamen Customs), filed an administrative lawsuit with the Xiamen Intermediate People's Court of Fujian Province.

The plaintiff alleged: On October 27, 2004, the defendant, Xiamen Customs, based on the fact that the plaintiff knowingly provided unloading and storage services for smuggled imported goods, issued Administrative Penalty Decision No. (2002) Xiamen Guan Cha Fa Zi 05-028 (hereinafter referred to as Decision No. 028) against the plaintiff pursuant to Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Implementing Rules for Administrative Penalties under the Customs Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules). The decision ordered confiscation of illegal gains of RMB 44,978,766 (hereinafter all amounts not otherwise specified are in RMB) and imposed a fine of RMB 10,000,000. First, because the import procedures for these oil products were incomplete, the plaintiff wrote to Xiamen Petroleum Corporation and also reported the matter to the defendant; the defendant's staff had coordinated on this matter and agreed to release these oil products, and Xiamen Petroleum Corporation also stated that it would be responsible for completing the Customs procedures and bearing the liability. Second, the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules were formulated and implemented for the Customs Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Customs Law) enacted and promulgated in 1987. By the time the defendant handled this case, the new Customs Law had already been enacted and implemented, and the old Customs Law and its relevant rules were no longer applicable. The defendant's application of the old rules to make the administrative penalty decision constituted a clear error in the applicable law. Third, the plaintiff obtained a total operating revenue of USD 5,797,142.97 from these transactions, equivalent to RMB 47,985,271; after deducting workers' wages, depreciation charges for warehousing equipment, and other necessary expenses of RMB 26,809,123, and after deducting taxes paid to the state of RMB 3,006,505, the plaintiff's income was only RMB 18,169,643. The defendant, having only deducted taxes from the operating revenue, treated all other operating expenses as illegal gains, which constituted an error in determining the composition and amount of "illegal gains." Fourth, the defendant not only confiscated the entire operating revenue after tax deduction as illegal gains, but also imposed a fine of RMB 10,000,000, making the penalty manifestly unjust. The plaintiff requests: 1. Revocation of the defendant's Decision No. 028, ordering the defendant to make a new specific administrative act within a time limit, or amendment of the defendant's administrative penalty decision; 2. An order that the defendant bear the litigation costs of this case.

The plaintiff, Botan Company, submitted Decision No. 028, the Administrative Reconsideration Decision (2004) No. 0037 of the General Administration of Customs of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the General Administration of Customs), and the receipt slip, to prove the existence of the specific administrative act challenged and that Botan Company filed the administrative lawsuit within the statutory time limit; it also submitted Botan Company's audit reports for 1997 and 1998, tax returns for 1997 and 1998, a list of expenses incurred for unloading and storing 64 shipments, and a statement of income calculation, to prove that Botan Company's total operating revenue included operating expenses and taxes paid.

The defendant argued: 1. Regarding the issue that Xiamen Petroleum Corporation failed to go through Customs declaration procedures for its imported oil products, although the plaintiff did report the matter to the defendant's staff at the beginning, and the defendant's staff orally replied that the goods could be released first and the procedures could be completed later, they also clearly stated that this should not be taken as a precedent, and that future goods could only be unloaded and stored with the Customs' consent. 2. The plaintiff is a large enterprise specializing in oil storage, and has an obligation to examine the lawful source of imported oil products. The plaintiff knew that the oil products it unloaded and stored had not undergone Customs declaration and tax payment procedures within China and were smuggled imported goods, yet it still proceeded to unload and store them to seek profit. The defendant, based on Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules, decided to impose an administrative penalty on the plaintiff. The applicable law was correct, and the penalty was appropriate. 3. On July 8, 2000, the 16th Session of the Standing Committee of the Ninth National People's Congress passed the "Decision on Amending the Customs Law of the People's Republic of China," which only amended the 1987 Customs Law without abolishing it. Although the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules were formulated based on the 1987 Customs Law, they had not been expressly repealed by the enacting authority at the time the defendant handled this case; as long as they did not conflict with the 2000 Customs Law, they should continue to be effective. 4. Conduct of knowingly failing to report and providing convenience to smugglers is illegal conduct, and illegal conduct should not be protected by law. The plaintiff naturally had to incur certain costs to carry out the illegal conduct, i.e., the operating expenses claimed by the plaintiff. However, such costs should not be protected by law; instead, the illegal actor must bear the costs based on the principle that one must suffer the consequences of one's own actions. If the illegal costs incurred by the actor were also protected, it would be tantamount to condoning the actor's illegal conduct. Therefore, the defendant was correct to calculate the plaintiff's other income after deducting the taxes paid to the state as illegal gains for confiscation. The plaintiff's claim that its illegal costs should be deducted lacks legal basis and should not be supported. The defendant's administrative penalty decision is correct and should be upheld by the court.

The defendant, Xiamen Customs, submitted the following evidence:

1. Business license of the legal person, to prove that Botan Company had the qualification to engage in oil storage business;
2. Correspondence between Botan Company and Xiamen Petroleum Corporation, to prove that Botan Company knew that the oil products were smuggled imported goods that had not undergone Customs declaration procedures, yet still proceeded to unload and store them, and failed to report to the Customs;
3. Diesel storage agreements signed between Botan Company, Xiamen Petroleum Corporation, and Xiamen Xiangyu New Earth Import & Export Co., Ltd., to prove that Botan Company allowed the oil products involved in the case to be unloaded and stored in its tank farm and collected illegal gains in return;
4. Statistics table on the unloading and storage of imported refined oil products, to prove the vessels, number of voyages, and quantities of smuggled oil products unloaded and stored at Botan Company's tank farm;
5. Evidence materials from the Customs' verification of imported oil products, to prove that from March 1997 to June 1998, 64 voyages of vessels including the "Hestia" transported oil products into China without going through Customs declaration and tax payment procedures;
6. Records of inquiries with Chen Yanxin, Lin Qizhi, Zeng Ming, Wu Yubo, and others, to prove that Botan Company allowed smuggled oil products to be unloaded and stored at its tank farm, knowing the facts and failing to report them;
7. Criminal rulings No. (2000) Min Xing Zhong Zi 604 and 613 of the Fujian High People's Court, to prove that the oil products involved in the case were smuggled goods;
8. Account statements between Botan Company and Xiamen Petroleum Corporation, and related income calculation certificates, to prove that Botan Company collected illegal gains totaling RMB 44,978,766 from unloading and storing smuggled oil products;
9. Tax payment receipts and lists, to prove that from May 1997 to June 1998, Botan Company paid a total of RMB 3,006,504.77 in taxes to the state;
10. Decision No. 028 and service record, Administrative Reconsideration Decision No. (2004) 0037 of the General Administration of Customs, hearing notice, hearing record, and administrative penalty notice, to prove that Xiamen Customs' administrative enforcement procedure was lawful;
11. Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules, to prove the legal basis for the administrative penalty.

The Xiamen Intermediate People's Court found the following facts through trial:

From March 1997 to June 1998, 64 voyages of vessels including the "Hestia" smuggled into China a total of 1,150,156.9 tons of diesel, 256,569.64 tons of crude soybean oil, 15,568.344 tons of crude rapeseed oil, 7,171.22 tons of palm oil, 30,008.01 tons of refined soybean oil, 5,633.231 tons of refined palm oil, and 15,945.921 tons of soybean oil, all of which had not undergone Customs declaration and tax payment procedures within China. These oil products were unloaded and stored at the tank farm owned by the plaintiff, Botan Company. Botan Company received USD 5,797,142.97 in revenue, equivalent to RMB 47,985,271, and paid taxes of RMB 3,006,505 to the state during this period. Based on this, on October 27, 2004, the defendant, Xiamen Customs, issued Decision No. 028, ordering the confiscation of Botan Company's illegal gains of RMB 44,978,766 and imposing a fine of RMB 10,000,000. On February 4, 2005, the General Administration of Customs issued Administrative Reconsideration Decision No. (2004) 0037, dismissing Botan Company's application for reconsideration and upholding Decision No. 028 made by Xiamen Customs.

It was further found that in March 1997, the plaintiff, Botan Company, wrote to Xiamen Petroleum Corporation, stating that the oil products that Xiamen Petroleum Corporation unloaded and stored at Botan Company had incomplete documentation and that Botan Company would not load them onto ships, requesting that Xiamen Petroleum Corporation provide Customs documents. On March 25, Xiamen Customs staff member Wu Yubo, while coordinating this matter, orally stated that the goods could be released first, but required Xiamen Petroleum Corporation to complete the Customs procedures later, and that this should not be taken as a precedent; future goods could only be unloaded and stored with the Customs' consent. On March 25 and April 1, Xiamen Petroleum Corporation replied to Botan Company, stating that it would handle the Customs procedures and bear the responsibility, and requested that Botan Company continue operations in the existing manner.

The issues in dispute in this case are: 1. Whether the application of Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules as the legal basis for Decision No. 028 was correct; 2. How Botan Company's conduct should be characterized; 3. Whether the determination of the amount of illegal gains in this case was appropriate.

The Xiamen Intermediate People's Court held:

The Customs Law is a law, and the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules are administrative regulations. Administrative regulations must, of course, comply with the law, but this does not mean that when a law is amended, the administrative regulations formulated under the pre-amendment law automatically become invalid. Regardless of whether the law has been amended, any provisions in administrative regulations formulated under the law that conflict with either the pre-amendment or post-amendment law are invalid. Other provisions only lose legal effect when repealed by a law, an administrative regulation, or an order of the State Council. On July 8, 2000, the 16th Session of the Standing Committee of the Ninth National People's Congress amended the Customs Law. On September 19, 2004, the State Council promulgated the "Regulations of the People's Republic of China on the Implementation of Customs Administrative Penalties," Article 68 of which provides: "These Implementing Regulations shall come into effect as of November 1, 2004. The 'Implementing Rules for Administrative Penalties under the Customs Law of the People's Republic of China,' as approved and revised by the State Council on February 17, 1993, and promulgated by the General Administration of Customs on April 1, 1993, shall be simultaneously repealed." Decision No. 028 was made before the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules were repealed, and the application of Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules as the legal basis was not improper in terms of applicable law.

As a large enterprise specializing in oil storage, the plaintiff, Botan Company, bears a statutory duty to examine whether the source of the imported oil products stored under Customs supervision is lawful. In fact, Botan Company initially refused to release the goods, indicating that it was aware of this duty. However, after that, Botan Company continued for a long period to unload, store, and release oil products without lawful sources, which is also a fact in this case. Botan Company's conduct falls within the circumstances described in Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules, i.e., "knowing the facts but failing to report and providing convenience to smugglers." Therefore, the defendant, Xiamen Customs, correctly made the penalty decision against the company. The coordination by individual Customs staff in this case and the reply from Xiamen Petroleum Corporation stating that it would bear the responsibility do not relieve Botan Company of its statutory duty and have no effect on the illegal nature of its conduct.

The total revenue of the plaintiff, Botan Company, from the illegal oil operations was RMB 47,985,271, which is undisputed by both parties. The above amount was obtained by Botan Company from illegal conduct, has a direct connection with the illegal conduct, and constitutes illegal gains. The defendant, Xiamen Customs, after deducting RMB 3,006,505 in taxes, confiscated the balance as illegal gains, which was not improper. Botan Company's claim that its operating expenses should be deducted lacks legal basis.

Accordingly, the Xiamen Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 54(1) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Administrative Procedure Law), rendered the following judgment on June 10, 2005:

Sustain the defendant Xiamen Customs' Administrative Penalty Decision No. (2002) Xiamen Guan Cha Fa Zi 05-028 made on October 27, 2004.

Court acceptance fee of RMB 284,903 shall be borne by the plaintiff, Botan Company.

After the first-instance judgment was pronounced, Botan Company, dissatisfied, appealed to the Fujian High People's Court, arguing: 1. After the appellant learned that the oil products had not undergone Customs declaration and tax payment procedures, it initially refused to release them and reported the matter to the appellee, the supervising authority. Subsequently, because the appellee's staff coordinated and proposed applying a "simplified procedure" for the oil products imported by Xiamen Petroleum Corporation, the appellant released the goods. The facts prove that the appellant was not aware of the smuggling activities of others, much less knowingly failed to report; rather, each release of goods was accompanied by clear instructions from the appellee authorizing the release. Therefore, the appellant's conduct does not fall within the circumstances described in Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules; 2. Only conduct that "colludes with smugglers to provide transportation, storage, mailing, or other convenience to smugglers" constitutes the conduct subject to penalty under Article 84 of the amended Customs Law. In contrast, Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules imposes penalties for conduct involving "knowing the facts but failing to report and providing convenience to smugglers." A comparison of the two provisions shows that the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules are stricter than the amended Customs Law and conflict with the amended Customs Law, and thus should not be applied in this case; 3. Article 17, Paragraph 2 of the Supreme People's Court's "Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Specific Application of Law in the Trial of Criminal Cases Involving Illegal Publications" provides: "The term 'amount of illegal gains' as used in this Interpretation refers to the amount of profit." Article 1 of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce's "Notice on the Method for Calculating Illegal Gains in Cases of Speculation and Illegal Business Activities" provides: "In production or business operations, where violations of national laws, regulations, or rules constitute speculation or illegal business activities, the method for calculating illegal gains is: where there is a purchase price and a sales price (including wholesale price and retail price), the difference between the sales price and the purchase price shall be the illegal gains; where the conduct involves production or processing, the difference between the sales price of the processed product and the cost price shall be the illegal gains." From the above judicial interpretation and administrative regulations, it can be seen that operating costs should be deducted from illegal gains. A reply from the Policy and Legal Affairs Department of the General Administration of Customs expresses the same opinion. 4. The appellee argues that the appellant has a statutory duty to examine the lawful source of the goods and that operating costs should not be deducted from illegal gains, but it has failed to provide the corresponding legal basis for these two claims, thereby failing to fulfill its burden of proof. The appellant requests that the first-instance judgment be reversed and that Decision No. 028 made by the appellee be revoked.

The appellee, Xiamen Customs, argued: 1. The facts of this case demonstrate that the appellant was aware of the Customs regulatory provisions; under such circumstances, the appellant still provided storage convenience for imported oil products without lawful documentation and failed to report to the Customs, which indeed falls within the circumstances described in Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules; 2. Although the amended Customs Law does not specifically mention that "knowing the facts but failing to report and providing convenience to smugglers" is subject to penalty, it provides that imported goods shall be subject to Customs supervision from the time of entry until Customs clearance is completed; enterprises engaged in warehousing of goods under Customs supervision shall handle receipt and delivery procedures in accordance with Customs regulations; those who collude with smugglers to provide transportation, storage, mailing, or other convenience to smugglers, if constituting a crime, shall be investigated for criminal liability; if not constituting a crime, the Customs shall confiscate the illegal gains and impose a fine. All of this demonstrates that regardless of whether under the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules or the amended Customs Law, the appellant's conduct was illegal. Furthermore, Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules only provides for administrative penalties against those who knowingly fail to report and provide convenience to smugglers, treating such conduct as a general illegal act; in contrast, the amended Customs Law uses the term "collusion," treating the provision of transportation, storage, mailing, or other convenience to smugglers as an act of complicity in smuggling, and those who commit such acts are primarily subject to criminal liability, with administrative penalties as a secondary consideration. In comparison, the amended Customs Law is naturally stricter. Since the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules do not conflict with the amended Customs Law and had not been repealed at the time the challenged administrative penalty decision was made, they are certainly applicable; 3. The term "illegal gains" as used in the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules refers to the total revenue obtained by the illegal actor from the illegal conduct. This should not be determined by the method used to calculate profits in lawful operations, nor should other provisions be used to interpret the meaning of "illegal gains" under the Customs Administrative Penalty Rules; 4. The appellee submitted legal bases to the court regarding the appellant's statutory duty to examine the lawful source of the goods and the confiscation of illegal gains, and has fulfilled its burden of proof. The appeal should be dismissed and the first-instance judgment upheld.

Fujian High People's Court found the following facts upon trial: On March 4, 1997, Wu Yubo, a staff member of the appellee Xiamen Customs, conducted coordination regarding the fact that the imported oil reported by Xiamen Petroleum General Company to the appellant Botan Company had gone through no customs declaration or tax payment procedures, resulting in a "meeting minutes." These "meeting minutes" were submitted to the court of first instance by Xiamen Customs as evidence, but were omitted from the judgment of first instance, and the time of this meeting was incorrectly found to be March 25, 1997, which should be corrected. Both parties have no objection to and should confirm the following facts: during the period from March 1997 to June 1998, the oil depot owned by Botan Company was a non-bonded oil depot and could not store bonded oil products; and that Xiamen Customs fulfilled its obligations of notification and hearing before making the administrative penalty decision under dispute in this case, and the penalty procedure was lawful. During the second instance, Botan Company applied for the retrieval of the letter No. Zhengfa Han [2003] 58 of the Policy and Regulation Department of the General Administration of Customs. Upon this application, the second instance inquired with the Policy and Regulation Department of the General Administration of Customs. Upon investigation, it was found that the Policy and Regulation Department of the General Administration of Customs had indeed produced the letter No. Zhengfa Han [2003] 58, which was a reply opinion made in response to the inquiry from the Industrial, Transport, and Commercial Affairs Department of the Legislative Affairs Office of the State Council regarding the meaning of "illegal gains," and had never been issued to local customs for implementation as an official document of the General Administration of Customs. Other facts found by the first instance are hereby confirmed as true.

The disputed issues of the second instance are:
1. Whether Botan Company's conduct falls within the circumstances stipulated in Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Detailed Rules for Customs Administrative Penalties?
2. Whether Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Detailed Rules for Customs Administrative Penalties conflicts with the amended Customs Law?
3. Whether illegal gains should include the operating expenses invested by the violator in committing the illegal act?

The Fujian High People's Court holds:

I. To determine whether the conduct of the appellant, Botan Company, falls within the circumstances stipulated in Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Detailed Rules for Customs Administrative Penalties, it should be examined whether its conduct simultaneously meets the two objective elements: knowing the facts but failing to report, and providing convenience to the smuggler.

Regarding knowing the facts but failing to report, this includes failing to report after knowing, as well as claiming ignorance as an excuse for not reporting when the party should have known. Determining whether a party should have known requires inferring whether the party subjectively recognized a certain fact based on factors such as the actor's level of knowledge, intellectual capacity, work ability, and professional competence. In a general sense, understanding the legal provisions of the relevant industry is an ability and basic requirement for any market entity participating in economic activities to conduct its business operations. In 1996, Liao Mingde, a staff member of Botan Company, in a fax replying to a legal consultation from Naser Bohlen of PAKTANK Asia Pacific Company, Hong Kong, clearly stated the legal provisions requiring that imported oil must go through customs declaration and tax payment procedures before being discharged and stored in a non-bonded oil depot. This indicates that as a large enterprise specializing in oil storage business, Botan Company was well aware of the legal provisions of China's Customs. In its specific business operations, Botan Company also acted in accordance with these legal provisions. For example, regarding the imported oil discharged and stored from the tanker "Pella" prior to the "Hestia," Botan Company had refused release because Xiamen Petroleum General Company failed to provide the corresponding customs documents. Subsequently, regarding the imported oil discharged and stored from the "Hestia," during the coordination by staff of the appellee Xiamen Customs, although the opinion was raised to apply a "simplified procedure" for release before completing the formalities, Xiamen Customs also required Xiamen Petroleum General Company, after completing the customs formalities, to deliver copies of the application form and the customs approval document to Botan Company as the basis for Botan Company to provide discharge and storage services. Regarding the oil discharged and stored subsequently from the "Hestia," Botan Company again refused release due to customs documentation issues, and reiterated the aforementioned coordination opinion of Xiamen Customs in a fax sent to Xiamen Petroleum General Company, repeatedly stating that the imported oil discharged into its depot should be goods on which customs duties had been paid, pointing out that "oil products imported from abroad will only be released for loading into the depot after obtaining written approval from Xiamen Customs." These facts prove that Botan Company had the ability to recognize that the conduct of Xiamen Petroleum General Company, which failed to produce customs approval documents and repeatedly discharged and stored imported oil in its operated depot, was illegal, and that the coordination opinion of Xiamen Customs had not misled or deceived Botan Company. However, Botan Company only repeatedly expressed its refusal to provide storage services, yet actually continued to provide storage services for the smuggled imported oil of Xiamen Petroleum General Company without reporting to Xiamen Customs, the regulatory authority. Botan Company ignored China's legal provisions, long provided storage convenience for imported oil without lawful documentation, and acquiesced in the occurrence and development of others' illegal acts. Subjectively, it was at fault; objectively, its conduct simultaneously satisfied the two elements of knowing the facts but failing to report and providing convenience to the smuggler, thereby violating Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Detailed Rules for Customs Administrative Penalties. Botan Company's appeal claim that it had reported the known facts to the regulatory authority and that each discharge, storage, and release of the involved oil was under clear instructions consented to by Xiamen Customs lacks corresponding evidence and shall not be supported.

II. The original Customs Law enacted and implemented in 1987 did not provide sufficiently detailed forms of smuggling crimes, especially regarding how liability should be borne among accomplices in smuggling, leading to many problems in practical operation. To implement the legal liability provisions of the original Customs Law, and authorized by its Article 60, the State Council approved the formulation and revision of the Detailed Rules for Customs Administrative Penalties. Article 6, Paragraph 1 thereof stipulates: "For smuggling acts committed by two or more persons jointly, penalties shall be imposed separately based on the distinction of circumstances and liabilities." Paragraph 2 stipulates: "If a person knows the facts but fails to report and provides convenience to the smuggler, the illegal gains shall be confiscated, and a fine of not more than twice the illegal gains may also be imposed." This article not only mentioned joint smuggling for the first time but also classified the conduct of "knowing the facts but failing to report and providing convenience to the smuggler" as joint smuggling for the first time. Article 156 of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Criminal Law), as amended on December 25, 1999, stipulates: "Whoever, in collusion with a smuggler of narcotic drugs, provides him with loans, funds, account numbers, invoices, certificates, or provides him with transportation, custody, mailing or other conveniences shall be punished as an accomplice in the crime of smuggling." To align with the amended Criminal Law, Article 84 of the amended Customs Law stipulates: "Whoever forges, alters, buys or sells customs documents, or in collusion with a smuggler provides the smuggler with loans, funds, account numbers, invoices, certificates, customs documents, or provides the smuggler with transportation, custody, mailing or other conveniences, if the act constitutes a crime, shall be investigated for criminal liability according to law; if the act does not constitute a crime, the customs shall confiscate the illegal gains and impose a fine." The term "collusion" is commonly used in criminal legislation to describe the relationship of joint offenders. For "collusion" to exist, the prerequisite must be knowledge, and knowledge includes the actor knowing or should have known. According to Article 84 of the amended Customs Law, if an actor knows or should have known that a smuggler is engaged in smuggling activities but still provides the smuggler with transportation, custody, mailing or other conveniences, it constitutes "collusion with the smuggler." In such a case, the criminal liability of the actor is first considered, followed by administrative penalties for those whose acts do not constitute a crime. Comparing the two, the provisions of Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Detailed Rules for Customs Administrative Penalties do not conflict with Article 84 of the amended Customs Law; they are merely less severe in terms of the degree of punishment than Article 84 of the amended Customs Law and are applicable to this case.

III. China is a socialist country governed by the rule of law. What conduct is illegal and what penalties are imposed on violators must be stipulated by relevant laws and regulations, and the specific provisions of various laws and regulations do not necessarily have a mutually applicable reference effect. The Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Specific Application of Law in the Trial of Criminal Cases of Illegal Publications is an interpretation of the issues of law application in the trial of such criminal cases by the people's courts and is limited to application when the people's courts try such criminal cases. The Notice of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce on Issues Concerning the Calculation Method of Illegal Gains in Cases of Illegal Speculation and Violations is also limited to application by the administrative authorities for industry and commerce when handling cases of illegal speculation and violations. Neither of the above two documents is related to the determination of illegal gains in smuggling cases. The reply letter from the Policy and Regulation Department of the General Administration of Customs is neither a law, regulation, rule, nor an interpretation issued by the General Administration of Customs for the specific application of laws, regulations, and rules. It is merely an expression of a viewpoint by an internal department of the General Administration of Customs on relevant legal issues and, according to law, cannot serve as the basis for adjudicating administrative cases. Moreover, these three documents do not provide clear or uniform standards on whether the operating expenses invested by the violator should be deducted from the illegal gains and therefore have no reference value. Article 6, Paragraph 2 of the Detailed Rules for Customs Administrative Penalties only stipulates that the illegal gains of a person who knows the facts but fails to report and provides convenience to the smuggler shall be confiscated, and does not stipulate that the operating expenses invested by the violator should be deducted from the illegal gains. The appellant Botan Company's claim that the aforementioned three documents should be referred to in this case and that its operating expenses should be deducted from the illegal gains lacks a legal basis and its arguments are not sustainable.

In conclusion, the Administrative Penalty Decision No. 028 made by the appellee Xiamen Customs complies with legal provisions and is correct. The first instance clearly found the facts, correctly applied the law, and the trial procedure was lawful; its judgment upholding Administrative Penalty Decision No. 028 was not improper. The appellant Botan Company's grounds for appeal lack corresponding factual basis and legal basis and are not sustainable. Accordingly, the Fujian High People's Court, pursuant to Article 61, Paragraph (1) of the Administrative Procedure Law, on October 14, 2005, adjudicated as follows:

Reject the appeal and affirm the original judgment.

The case acceptance fee for the second instance of this case is RMB 284,903, to be borne by the appellant Botan Company.

This judgment is final.
